ety.text: From Middle English losen, from Old English losian. The modern pronunciation with /uː/ (instead of the /oʊ~əʊ/ that would be expected from Early Modern /ɔː/) is due to conflation with loose.

senses.d: To cease to have (something) in one's possession or capability.
ex: If you lose that ten-pound note, you'll be sorry.
He lost his hearing in the explosion.

senses.d: To have (an organ) removed from one's body, especially by accident.
ex: Johnny lost a tooth, but kept it for the tooth fairy.
He lost his spleen in a car wreck.

senses.d: To shed (weight).
ex: I’ve lost five pounds this week.

senses.d: To experience the death of (someone to whom one has an attachment, such as a relative or friend).
ex: She lost all her sons in the war.

senses.d: To pay or owe (some wager) due from an unsuccessful bet or gamble.
ex: Frank had lost $500 staying in Vegas.

senses.d: To be deprived of (some right or privileged access to something).
ex: Users who engage in disruptive behavior may lose their accounts.

senses.d: To wander from; to miss, so as not to be able to find; to go astray from.
ex: I lost my way in the forest.
He hath lost his fellows.

senses.d: To become a defeated competitor in (a game, competition, trial, etc).
ex: We lost the football match.
You just lost The Game.

senses.d: To be defeated (in a game, competition, contest, etc.)
ex: The team scored four goals but still managed to lose.

senses.d: To be unable to follow or trace (somebody or something) any longer.
ex: The policeman lost the robber he was chasing.
Mission control lost the satellite as its signal died down.

grp.label: cease to have in one's possession or capability
experience the death of (someone to whom one has an attachment, such as a relative or friend)
be unable to follow or trace (somebody or something) any longer

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French perdre, from Old French perdre, from Latin perdere.
Inherited from Latin perdere. The variant past participle perso was created by analogy with preso, etc.
Borrowed from Old French esmarrir, from marir (“to frustrate, to sadden”), from Frankish *marrijan.
Inherited from Old Spanish perder, inherited from Latin perdere, whence also English perdition.

pt:perder.gl: to lose (an object, a job, interest etc.)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese perder, from Latin perdere. The first person singular form in the present indicative and all forms of the present subjunctive and commands (except the second person informal affirmative commands) have an analogous change from D to C (expected "perdo" instead of "perco," for example).

pt:emagrecer.gl: to become leaner; to lose body weight

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enmagrecer, from Late Latin ēmacrēscere, from Latin macer (“lean”), from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. By surface analysis, e- + magro + -ecer.
Borrowed from Italian fracassare. Compare English fracas.

pt:perder de vista.gl: to lose sight of (to be no longer able to see)

phr: and nothing of value was lost
how you get them is how you lose them

ety.text: From Middle English loste, losede (preterite) and Middle English lost, ilost, ilosed (past participle), from Old English losode (preterite) and Old English losod, ġelosod, equivalent to lose + -t.

senses.d: Having wandered from, or unable to find, the way.
ex: The children were soon lost in the forest.

senses.d: In an unknown location; unable to be found.
ex: Deep beneath the ocean, the Titanic was lost to the world.

senses.d: Not perceptible to the senses; no longer visible.
ex: an island lost in a fog; a person lost in a crowd

senses.d: Parted with; no longer held or possessed.
ex: a lost limb; lost honour

senses.d: Not employed or enjoyed; thrown away; employed ineffectually; wasted; squandered.
ex: a lost day; a lost opportunity or benefit; no time should be lost

senses.d: Ruined or destroyed, either physically or morally; past help or hope.
ex: a ship lost at sea; a woman lost to virtue; a lost soul

senses.d: Hardened beyond sensibility or recovery; alienated; insensible.
ex: lost to shame; lost to all sense of honour

senses.d: Occupied with, or under the influence of, something, so as not to notice external things.
ex: to be lost in thought

ety.text: Inherited from Latin perditus.

phr: be lost to the four winds

chain.g: to cut, sunder, separate, loose, lose

ety.text: From Middle English los, from Old English los (“damage, destruction, loss”), from Proto-West Germanic *los, from Proto-Germanic *lusą (“dissolution, break-up, loss”), from Proto-Indo-European *lews- (“to cut, sunder, separate, loose, lose”). Cognate with Icelandic los (“dissolution, looseness, break-up”), Old English lor, forlor (“loss, ruin”), Middle High German verlor (“loss, ruin”). More at lose.

senses.d: The result of no longer possessing an object, a function, or a characteristic due to external causes or misplacement.
ex: loss of limb; weight loss; loss of cognitive functions; loss of appetite.
People are less willing to take a risk to make a gain than to avoid a loss.

senses.d: The destruction or ruin of an object.
Something that has been destroyed or ruined.
ex: It was a terrible crash; both cars were total losses.

senses.d: Defeat; an instance of being defeated.
ex: The match ended in their first loss of the season.

senses.d: The death of a person or animal.
ex: We mourn his loss.
The battle was won, but losses were great.

senses.d: The condition of grief caused by losing someone or something, especially someone who has died.
ex: Her daughter's sense of loss eventually led to depression.

senses.d: The sum an entity loses on balance.
ex: The sum of expenditures and taxes minus total income is a loss, when this difference is positive.

senses.d: Electricity of kinetic power expended without doing useful work.
ex: The inefficiency of many old-fashioned power plants exceeds 60% loss before the subsequent losses during transport over the grid.

grp.label: the result of no longer possessing something
the death of a person or animal
grief caused by losing someone or something
financial: the sum lost on balance

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French perte, from Old French perte, from the feminine of Latin perditus. Compare Italian perdita and Spanish pérdida.
From Latin perdita, the feminine of perditus. Compare French perte, Portuguese perda, and Spanish pérdida.

From Vulgar Latin *perdita, from the feminine of Latin perditus. Coromines & Pascual regard it as a semi-learned rather than popular form. Romance cognates include Portuguese perda, Italian perdita, French perte.
From Old Galician-Portuguese perda, from Vulgar Latin *perdita, from the feminine of Latin perditus (“lost”), perfect passive participle of perdō (“to lose”).
From Middle French desfaicte, from Old French desfaite. Cognate with English defeat.

ety.text: Borrowed from French déroute (“rout”), from Old French desroter (“to disband, to disperse”), from rote, route (“band, company, troop, group of armed men”), originally a substantivized feminine of rout (literally “broken”), from Latin ruptus, perfect passive participle of rumpō (“to break”).
Inherited from Latin mortem, from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).
From Latin lūctus. Compare Spanish and Portuguese luto.
Nominalization of Etymology 1.
From Latin passivus.
From Middle English loser, losere, equivalent to lose + -er. In the sense of contemptible or worthless individual, perhaps an alteration of losel, which see.

senses.d: A person who loses; one who fails to win or thrive.
ex: In a two-horse race there is always one winner and one loser.
He was always a good loser.

senses.d: Something of poor quality.
A person who is frequently unsuccessful in life.
ex: That guy is a born loser!
I'm a constant loser in love.

senses.d: A contemptible or unfashionable person.
One who or that which loses something, such as extra weight, car keys, etc.
A losing proposition, one that is likely to lose or already has lost (such as a losing bet or, analogously, a predictably fruitless task or errand).
ex: In terms of betting on outcomes, Mars is a clear loser.

senses.d: A person convicted of a crime, especially more than once.
ex: He's a three-time loser doing twenty years.

grp.label: person who is frequently unsuccessful in life
